item.title: Kagoshima Imo Shochu — Guide
item.description: Shochu, a distilled Japanese spirit, is deeply woven into Kagoshima’s culture, and the prefecture is the undisputed heartland of imo-jōchū — shochu made from sweet potato (satsumaimo), the region’s signature crop. Unlike clear, neutral vodka, imo shochu has a distinctive, richly aromatic and earthy character with a hint of natural sweetness, and comes in a huge variety of styles from countless local distilleries, each with its own flavour. Kagoshima has hundreds of shochu makers, and many traditional distilleries (especially around Kirishima and Makurazaki) welcome visitors for tours explaining the sweet-potato brewing process, followed by tastings.

item.title: Aizu-Wakamatsu Sake: Brewery Tours & Tastings — Guide
item.description: Aizu-Wakamatsu has been one of Japan’s premier sake-brewing regions for centuries, its combination of pure mountain snowmelt water, rice-growing plains and bitterly cold winters creating ideal conditions for fermentation. Several historic breweries in and around the city, some dating back over 100 years, open their doors for tours explaining the brewing process, followed by tastings of a range of styles from dry (karakuchi) to fruity ginjo varieties, often in atmospheric wooden kura (storehouse) buildings.

item.title: Awamori Guide: Okinawa's Spirit, Tasting & Izakaya
item.description: Awamori is Okinawa’s traditional distilled spirit and the oldest distilled liquor in Japan, with roots reaching back over 500 years to Ryukyu Kingdom trade. Made from long-grain Thai rice and black koji mould unique to Okinawa, it’s stronger and more characterful than mainland shochu. Aged versions, called kusu, mellow over years into something prized and complex. Sipping awamori at an izakaya — neat, on the rocks or in a highball — is one of the great pleasures of an Okinawan evening.
